## 1. Introduction

You may have heard about the linux program [htop](https://htop.dev/), it is an **interactive process viewer** for Unix-like systems.

With `htop` you can:

-   See a **real-time overview** of system processes, CPU cores, memory, and swap usage.
-   **Scroll and search** through processes easily.
-   Interactively **sort, filter, and kill processes** with simple key commands.
-   Get a quick sense of **system health** thanks to its bars and colors.

Below is a screenshot of how it looks:

![](images/htop.png)

On this activity you are going to build your own simplified version of `htop` by writing python code that analyzes the contents of `/proc`. Once finished, it will look like this:

![](images/amsatop.jpg)

## 3. Outline

This activity is split onto 3 incremental parts, which are going to be related to the contents explained during the different classes.

1.  On the first week, once we have explained **syscalls, processes and ProcFS**, your job will be to implement a function that retrieves a list of all the system processes.

2.  Next, after having explained **process priorities**, we'll want you to get the priority of each of the processes.

3.  Finally, since you'll understand the **SIGHUP signal**, the idea is that you also find out which processes are ignoring this signal or not.

## 5. Tasks

Below is a detailed explanation of what you have to do on each task, but before reading through we want to make something clear:

On each of the following tasks you'll be obtaining a list of processes and then looking for further information on these processes.

Notice that if I get a list of all the processes currently active on my system, and then I go fetch information on them, it may have happened that **one of these processes has ended and its information is no longer available**. Your code has to be prepared for this scenario and be prepared to not find any information about a given process because it is no longer running and thus there is nothing for that process inside `/proc`.

In that case just exclude the process from the returned list. Be aware that some tests already check that, so don't bother too much.

### PRAC-2.1: Getting all processes

Implement [the get_processes method](https://github.com/El-Despatx/amsatop-template/blob/main/src/myhtop/amsatop_solution.py#L11) so it returns a list where each element is an instance of [`Process`](https://lleida.amsa.udl.cat/docs/_apidoc/amsatop.html#amsatop.Process). There has to be an element on the list for each **process, thread and kthread** running on the system.

This part has to be done exclusively by reading the raw contents of `/proc`. It is **strictly forbidden to use any external libraries or commands**.

When creating instances of `Process`, notice that the field `priority` can be `None`. As stated on the docs:

> Can be None if unavailable or you’re doing Prac-2.1.

When working on Prac-2.1 just set that field to `None`.

::: callout-tip
Make sure to read through [the docs](https://lleida.amsa.udl.cat/docs/_apidoc/amsatop.utils.html) of the helper classes and functions, we promise using them will make your life easier 😉!
:::

::: {.callout-important title="**Very very important 🚨**"}
It is **very important** that you make use of the property [proc_folder](https://lleida.amsa.udl.cat/docs/_apidoc/amsatop.html#amsatop.Htop.proc_folder) of the [Htop](https://lleida.amsa.udl.cat/docs/_apidoc/amsatop.html#amsatop.Htop) class when accessing files on `"/proc"`. **Do not use a hardcoded string "/proc"**, instead use `self.proc_folder` (which is a string that defaults to "/proc"). This is essential for the tests to work.

Here is an example of **what NOT to do**:

``` {.python code-line-numbers="true"}
class Amsatop(Htop):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def get_processes(self) -> List[Process]:
        for entry in os.listdir("/proc"): # Do NOT do it like this ❌
            if ...
```

Here is an example of **what you should do**:

``` {.python code-line-numbers="true"}
class Amsatop(Htop):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def get_processes(self) -> List[Process]:
        for entry in os.listdir(self.proc_folder): # Do it like this ✅
            if ...
```
:::

#### Hints about how to get the differents processes/threads/kthreads from /proc.

As stated on the [week-2 slides](/weeks/week-2.html#/procfs), there are different ways to get information about /proc. We recommend you to use the following ones:

-   To detect processes or kernel threads, the algorithm is "trivial", the idea is:

    1)  List the contents of the proc directory, and filter the ones that are digits (pids/tgid).
    2)  Now you have to filter if they're a process or kernel thread. We recommend you to [apply the mask](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AHiepE54l88) that the [htop code applies to the flags content](/weeks/week-2.html#/properties-of-procfs-kernel-threads) to see if they are a kernel thread [^1].

    -   If it's a kernel thread, add it to the list and stop analyzing.
    -   If it's a process, add it, but be aware that can have threads spawned (next point will explain this).

-   To detect threads, it's a little bit more complicated, you should:

    -   For each detected process, inspect the tasks folder. Be aware that:
        -   This folder will have, at least, one entry, which should be equal to the pid of the current process.
        -   If it has more than one entry, it means it has some thread spawned.

[^1]: Remember, that in c, applying a mask would be

    ``` {.c code-line-numbers="true"}
    /* Not exposed yet. Defined at include/linux/sched.h */
    #ifndef PF_KTHREAD
    #define PF_KTHREAD 0x00200000
    #endif
    // More code here...
    if (lp->flags & PF_KTHREAD) {
    proc->isKernelThread = true;
    }
    ```

    In python, the **exact** same code would look like this:

    ``` {.python code-line-numbers="true"}
    ...
    PF_KTHREAD = 0x00200000
    if (lp.flags & PF_KTHREAD) != 0:
       proc.isKernelThread = True
    ```

### Prac-2.2: Adding priorities

Implement [get_priorities method](https://github.com/El-Despatx/amsatop-template/blob/main/src/myhtop/amsatop_solution.py#L14) so it returns a list of [Process](https://lleida.amsa.udl.cat/docs/_apidoc/amsatop.html#amsatop.Process). It has to be the same list we obtained on **Prac-2.1** but now we want you to set the value of the `priority` field if available.

There are no hints here.... It should be pretty easy to implement if you already have Prac-2.1 solved.

Play with the `nice` command so you can see how the priorities change on real time!
:::

::: {.callout-important title="**Don't worry too much!🚨**"}
It's normal to see some "strange" priorities on kernel threads!!
:::

### Prac-2.3: Filtering where SIGHUP is ignored

Implement [the get_hup method](https://github.com/El-Despatx/amsatop-template/blob/main/src/myhtop/amsatop_solution.py#L17) so it returns a list of [Process](https://lleida.amsa.udl.cat/docs/_apidoc/amsatop.html#amsatop.Process). It has to be the same list we obtained on **Prac-2.2 (with the priorities)** but now we want to add a filter so only those processes that are ignoring the `SIGHUP` signal are returned, those that are not ignoring it are expected to **not be present on the returned list**. Be aware that **ignoring a signal is not the same as handling a signal**.

#### Hints about detecting signals










As we've seen in class, processes can **ignore signals**. But how can we find out which signals a process is ignoring?

Lukily, Linux gives us this information!

One of the files inside the process /proc/{pid} has a SigIgn (signal ignore) field which shows the set of signals the process is currently ignoring. Retrieving this information works in much the same way as checking whether a PID/TID corresponds to a kernel thread (by examining and interpreting bitmasks). This field could be for example:

```text
SigIgn: 0000000000000005
```

This might look like a strange number, but it's actually quite simple!

##### Step 1: Understanding `SigIgn`

`SigIgn` is a **bitmap represented in hexadecimal**.

A bitmap is just a binary number where **each bit represents something different**.

In our case, each bit represents one signal:

- `1` means the signal is being ignored.
- `0` means the signal is NOT being ignored.

The bits correspond to signal numbers, **counting from right to left**:

```text
Signal:  8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1
         | | | | | | | |
Binary:  0 0 0 0 0 1 0 1
```

In this example:

- Signal 1 (`SIGHUP`) is ignored.
- Signal 2 (`SIGINT`) is NOT ignored.
- Signal 3 (`SIGQUIT`) is ignored.

::: {.callout-note}
Remember that `SigIgn` is written in **hexadecimal**, not binary!

For example, hexadecimal `5` is `101` in binary. The zeros on the left don't change the number.
:::

##### Step 2: How do we check a specific signal?

Imagine that we want to know whether **signal 3** is ignored.

We could convert `SigIgn` into binary and look at the third bit from the right.

But there's an easier way to do this in Python: **using a mask**!

A mask is simply another binary number that has a `1` in the position we want to check, and `0` everywhere else.

For example:

```text
Signal:  8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1
         | | | | | | | |
Mask:    0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0
```

Since we're interested in signal 3, our mask is `00000100`, which is **4 in decimal**.

How can we calculate the mask for any signal?

Notice this pattern:

| Signal number | Mask in binary | Mask in decimal |
|---------------|----------------|-----------------|
| 1             | 00000001       | 1               |
| 2             | 00000010       | 2               |
| 3             | 00000100       | 4               |
| 4             | 00001000       | 8               |
| 5             | 00010000       | 16              |

Every time we move one position to the left, the value doubles. Therefore, we can calculate the mask for signal number `N` with:

$$
\text{mask} = 2^{N-1}
$$

##### Step 3: Using the mask to check the signal

Now that we have our mask, we are going to use the **bitwise AND operator (`&`)**.

This operator compares two binary numbers, bit by bit. The result has a `1` only in positions where **both numbers have a `1`**.

Let's try it with our example:

```text
SigIgn:  0 0 0 0 0 1 0 1    (5)
Mask:    0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0    (4)
         -----------------
Result:  0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0    (4)
```

The result is **4**, which means that the bit corresponding to signal 3 was set to `1`, so **signal 3 is ignored**.

What if we check signal 2 instead?

```text
SigIgn:  0 0 0 0 0 1 0 1    (5)
Mask:    0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0    (2)
         -----------------
Result:  0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0    (0)
```

The result is **0**, meaning signal 2 is NOT ignored.

::: {.callout-tip}
The important thing to remember:

- If `SigIgn & mask` is **zero**, the signal is NOT ignored.
- If `SigIgn & mask` is **not zero**, the signal IS ignored.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Example: Using a bitmask in Python"}

```python
number = 11 # Value of the bitmap
mask   = 4  # We want to check the second bit

result = number & mask

if result != 0:
    print("The bit is set to 1!")
else:
    print("The bit is set to 0!")
```

The `&` operator compares each bit:

```text
  1011   (number)
& 0010   (mask)
------
  0010   (result)
```

If the result is **not zero**, the bit we're checking is set to `1`.

:::



##### Step 4: Applying this to PRAC-2.3

Your task is to use this idea to filter the processes obtained in PRAC-2.2, returning **only the processes that ignore SIGHUP**.

::: {.callout-important}
**Ignoring a signal is NOT the same as handling it!**

- `SigIgn` tells us which signals are **ignored**.
- `SigCgt` tells us which signals have a **custom handler**.
:::

For PRAC-2.3, we only care about `SigIgn`.

Keep in mind that [each signal corresponds to a number...](https://faculty.cs.niu.edu/~hutchins/csci480/signals.htm)

::: {.callout-important title="**Don't worry too much!🚨**"}
It's normal to see some `kthreads` ignoring SIGHUP!! Don't worry too much about it!
:::

## 6. Setting the environment up!

### Installing libfuse

We use a Linux feature called FUSE in our tests. This lets us emulate the special capabilities of the /proc filesystem without bothering you (the student) with the technical details of our test setup.

For this reason, in the virtual machine’s command line, **you must run the following command for the tests to work**:

``` bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install libfuse2t64
```

### Cloning the repository and set it up:

Remember that, once you forked the Github repository on [section 2](act-2.qmd#delivery), you will have to clone your repository with [^2]:

[^2]: If you don't have any idea of what we're talking about, revisit the [setting up the VM and brief git summary](/resources/vm_git.qmd)

``` bash
git clone <ssh_address_of_your_git_repository>
```

Then, enter inside the folder of the repository and setup a virtual environment for the python project, this will be done with:

``` bash
uv sync
```

And then, you can enable the virtualenv on your current shell (zsh or bash) with:

``` bash
source .venv/bin/activate 
```

### Running tests:

You can run all the tests we give to you with the following command (from the project root path):

``` bash
uv run pytest
```

You can also run specific test-suites for each prac, for example:

``` bash
# For prac 2.1:
uv run pytest test/prac_2_1

# For prac 2.2:
uv run pytest test/prac_2_2

# For prac 2.3:
uv run pytest test/prac_2_3
```

### \[Optional\] Running tests with coverage:

If you want to see if all the lines of your code are covered by the tests (this is usually a good indicator), you can run a test coverage, this will display information about the relationship between your code and our tests! Run:

``` bash
uv run coverage run -m pytest  -v -s
uv run coverage report
```

::: callout-tip
Learn more about [pytest options here](/resources/pytest.qmd)
:::

## 8. Rules

1.  **No external python libraries** can be used, only `amsatop` and built-in libraries are allowed (e.g `os`, `typing`).
2.  It is **forbidden to make python execute a Linux command** that will provide the information about processes.
3.  The process information needed can **only be obtained by reading the contents of `/proc` and parsing it out** (remember you have [helpers](https://lleida.amsa.udl.cat/docs/_apidoc/amsatop.utils.html) for that).
4.  Make sure the tests are passing on the [Ubuntu VM](https://amsa.lol/#resources), we'll pass them on the VM too.
5.  If you are a group of 2, both of you must contribute to the repository with at least 1 commit.
